section.title: Consecration of the Firstborn
section.sectionRationale: Before Israel takes a single step toward the sea, the LORD claims the firstborn as His own and fixes the Feast of Unleavened Bread as a permanent, embodied lesson for the generations to come. Redemption is meant to be taught, worn, and remembered, not merely experienced once.
section.thesis: Because the LORD spared Israel's firstborn at the cost of Egypt's, every firstborn now belongs to Him, redeemed rather than kept, and the whole family is to carry the story of that mighty deliverance on their hands, on their foreheads, and onto their children.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the command to consecrate every firstborn; Moses' instructions for keeping the Feast of Unleavened Bread as a sign and teaching moment; and the specific rule for redeeming the firstborn of donkeys and of sons.

units.label: Consecrate the firstborn
units.note: every firstborn belongs to the LORD

verses.text: Then the LORD said to Moses,
“{{consecrate|Consecrate}} to Me every firstborn male. The firstborn from every womb among the Israelites belongs to Me, both of man and beast.”

units.label: Remember this day
units.note: unleavened bread, and a sign taught to the children

verses.text: So Moses told the people, “Remember this day, the day you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; for the LORD brought you out of it by the strength of His hand. And nothing leavened shall be eaten.
Today, in the month of Abib, you are leaving.

And when the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, and Jebusites, the land He swore to your fathers that He would give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you shall keep this service in this month.
For seven days you are to eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day there shall be a feast to the LORD.
Unleavened bread shall be eaten during those seven days. Nothing leavened may be found among you, nor shall leaven be found anywhere within your borders.
And on that day you are to explain to your son, ‘This is because of what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.’
It shall be a {{sign|sign}} for you on your hand and a reminder on your forehead that the Law of the LORD is to be on your lips. For with a mighty hand the LORD brought you out of Egypt.
Therefore you shall keep this statute at the appointed time year after year.

units.label: Redeeming the firstborn
units.note: a lamb for the donkey, a son redeemed

verses.text: And after the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites and gives it to you, as He swore to you and your fathers,
you are to present to the LORD the firstborn male of every womb. All the firstborn males of your livestock belong to the LORD.
You must {{redeem|redeem}} every firstborn donkey with a lamb, and if you do not redeem it, you are to break its neck. And every firstborn of your sons you must redeem.
In the future, when your son asks you, ‘What does this mean?’ you are to tell him, ‘With a mighty hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

And when Pharaoh stubbornly refused to let us go, the LORD killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both of man and beast. This is why I sacrifice to the LORD the firstborn male of every womb, but I redeem all the firstborn of my sons.’
So it shall serve as a sign on your hand and a symbol on your forehead, for with a mighty hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt.”

consecrate.gloss: To set apart as holy, to dedicate to God's exclusive use. The firstborn already belonged to the LORD in principle since He spared them in Egypt; now Israel is told to formally set them apart, acknowledging in ritual what is already true.

sign.gloss: A sign, a visible marker of a deeper reality. Later Jewish tradition took the command to bind this as a sign on the hand and forehead quite literally, in tefillin; whether literal or figurative, the point is that redemption must be kept visibly present before the worshiper.

redeem.gloss: To buy back, to ransom, to release by paying a price or substitute. A firstborn donkey is redeemed with a lamb or its neck is broken; a firstborn son is always redeemed, never sacrificed, because in Israel human life is never the payment, only pictured by a substitute.

basic.context: Right after Israel leaves Egypt, before they even reach the sea, God tells Moses that every firstborn now belongs to Him, because He spared Israel's firstborn at the cost of Egypt's. Along with that comes the Feast of Unleavened Bread, a yearly reminder they are to explain to their children.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes actual instructions given to Israel for their ongoing worship and family teaching. Christians are not bound to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread or redeem literal firstborn sons, but the underlying principle endures: God's mighty acts of redemption are to be remembered, taught to children, and kept visibly present in daily life.
basic.originalLanguages: To qadash, consecrate, the firstborn is to set them apart as belonging to God alone, acknowledging what His deliverance already made true. The instruction to wear this as an ot, a sign, on hand and forehead insists that redemption not stay a private memory but shape daily, visible life. And to padah, redeem, a firstborn is to substitute something else, a lamb or a price, in its place.
basic.typology: Every firstborn son in Israel is redeemed, never sacrificed, because a substitute always stands in his place, just as the Passover lamb once stood in the place of Israel's firstborn in Egypt. This repeated pattern of substitution prepares the way for the ultimate substitute, Christ, who redeems His people at the cost of His own life.
basic.christ: Luke's Gospel deliberately echoes this chapter when Mary and Joseph present the infant Jesus in the temple to fulfill the law of the firstborn, Luke 2:22-23. Jesus, the true firstborn, is not redeemed by a substitute but becomes the substitute Himself, the price paid so that many sons and daughters are set free.
basic.god: God claims what He has already saved; He does not merely rescue and move on but insists that the rescued live as people who belong to Him. He is also endlessly patient with the ordinary work of teaching, expecting parents to explain and children to ask, generation after generation.
basic.crossReferences: Luke 2:22-23 shows Jesus presented according to this very law of the firstborn. Numbers 3:11-13 later assigns the Levites to stand in the place of Israel's firstborn. Deuteronomy 6:6-9 echoes the same command to bind God's words on hand and forehead and teach them to children.
basic.oneStory: God claims a redeemed people as His own and commands that their story be worn, spoken, and passed on, not simply remembered in private. This becomes the shape of the whole Bible's call to the redeemed: live visibly as those who belong to God, and teach the next generation the mighty hand that set you free.

context.literary:
Exodus 13:1-16 is built as a frame. It opens with a two-verse word from the LORD to Moses about the firstborn, verses 1 and 2, and then Moses addresses the people in a speech of two matching halves. The first half, verses 3 to 10, concerns the Feast of Unleavened Bread; the second, verses 11 to 16, concerns the firstborn. Each half begins with the same condition, 'when the LORD brings you into the land,' verses 5 and 11. Each includes a child's question or a parent's explanation, verses 8 and 14. Each ends with a sign on the hand and a reminder or symbol on the forehead, and with the phrase 'with a mighty hand the LORD brought you out of Egypt,' verses 9 and 16. The repetition is deliberate, the kind of structure meant to be memorised and recited.

The passage looks backward and forward at once. It stands between the departure from Rameses, Exodus 12:37, and the crossing of the sea, Exodus 14. Israel has not yet escaped Pharaoh's army, and yet Moses is already speaking of life in Canaan and of children not yet born. Faith is being taught to assume that God will finish what He began.

The movement of the unit also runs from God's claim to the family's confession. It opens with the divine assertion, 'belongs to Me,' verse 2, and it closes with the father's words, 'This is why I sacrifice to the LORD the firstborn male of every womb, but I redeem all the firstborn of my sons,' verse 15. What God declares in verse 2 each household is to own in the first person. The father's 'I' in verse 15 matches his 'me' in verse 8: 'what the LORD did for me when I came out of Egypt.' The story is to be told not as distant history but as personal testimony.

The phrase 'strength of hand' or 'mighty hand' comes four times, verses 3, 9, 14 and 16. It has already appeared in Exodus 3:19 and 6:1, and it will become one of Deuteronomy's favourite ways of describing the exodus, Deuteronomy 5:15, 6:21 and 26:8.
context.historical:
The law of the firstborn touched every family and every flock. The firstborn male of cattle, sheep and goats was to be given to the LORD, which in later practice meant it was sacrificed and its meat given to the priests, Numbers 18:17-18. Unclean animals such as the donkey could not be offered. They had to be redeemed with a lamb or else killed, verse 13, so that the LORD's claim could not be dodged by keeping the animal. The donkey was the working animal of an ordinary household, and the choice between paying a lamb and losing the donkey made the claim costly.

Firstborn sons were never to be sacrificed. Israel lived among peoples who did at times offer children to their gods. Scripture records the king of Moab sacrificing 'his firstborn son, who was to succeed him,' 2 Kings 3:27, and the law forbids Israel to give any child to Molech, Leviticus 18:21. The prophets condemn Israelites who adopted the practice, and the LORD says it was 'something I never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind,' Jeremiah 7:31. Against that background the command 'every firstborn of your sons you must redeem' is a sharp line between the LORD and the gods of Canaan.

The redemption of sons was later regulated. At Sinai the LORD took the Levites in place of the firstborn of Israel, Numbers 3:12-13 and 8:16-18. When the firstborn were counted there were 22,273, and the 273 who exceeded the number of Levites were redeemed at five shekels each, Numbers 3:43-51. Later firstborn sons were redeemed at a month old for five shekels of silver, Numbers 18:16.

The month of Abib, verse 4, takes its name from the ripening ears of barley. Exodus 9:31 uses the same word when it says the barley 'was ripe.' After the exile the month was known by its Babylonian name Nisan, Nehemiah 2:1. Verse 5 names five peoples of Canaan, and 'a land flowing with milk and honey' repeats the promise of Exodus 3:8. By the first century the command of verses 9 and 16 was observed by wearing small boxes containing texts of Scripture, which Jesus calls 'phylacteries,' Matthew 23:5.
context.canonical:
The claim of verse 2 recurs throughout the law. It is repeated in the covenant code, 'You are to give Me the firstborn of your sons,' Exodus 22:29, and in the renewed covenant after the golden calf, Exodus 34:19-20, where the redemption of the donkey and the sons is restated word for word. Numbers 3:13 and 8:17 explain it as a direct result of the Passover: 'On the day I struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, I consecrated to Myself all the firstborn in Israel.' Numbers 18:15-16 fixes the redemption price.

The command to teach children and bind the words on hand and forehead is taken up in Deuteronomy 6:6-9 and 11:18-20, where it applies not only to the exodus but to the whole law. Deuteronomy 6:20-25 gives a child's question and a father's answer that closely follow Exodus 13:14. Joshua 4:6-7 and 4:21-24 use the same pattern for the stones from the Jordan. Psalm 78:4-7 turns it into a principle of generations: God 'commanded our fathers to teach to their children.' Proverbs 3:3, 6:21 and 7:3 apply the image of binding to wisdom.

The theme of the firstborn runs through Scripture. Israel is God's firstborn son, Exodus 4:22. Jeremiah 31:9 says 'Ephraim is My firstborn.' Psalm 89:27 promises of David's line, 'I will indeed appoint him as My firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth.' The prophets also warn against pagan distortions of the firstborn law, Micah 6:7.

In the New Testament, Luke 2:22-23 records that Jesus' parents presented Him at the temple, quoting 'Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord,' the text the BSB footnote at Exodus 13:2 links to Luke. Paul calls Christ 'the firstborn over all creation' and 'firstborn from among the dead,' Colossians 1:15 and 1:18, and 'the firstborn among many brothers,' Romans 8:29. Hebrews 12:23 describes the church as 'the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven.' Revelation contrasts the mark of the beast 'on their right hand or on their forehead,' Revelation 13:16, with the Lamb's name 'written on their foreheads,' Revelation 14:1.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wanted Israel to see that their deliverance created an obligation. The firstborn were spared because the LORD had passed over them, and verse 15 draws the conclusion: what God spared, God claims. Every time a firstborn animal was offered or a firstborn son redeemed, the household would be reminded that its life was owed to the LORD.

He also wanted the exodus to be remembered in a way that could not fade. Israel was about to leave Egypt behind; within a generation there would be people who had never seen Pharaoh. So Moses tied the memory to the rhythms of the year, a week of bread without leaven, and to the rhythms of family life, the birth of the first son or the first calf. The memory would be renewed by events no family could avoid.

And he wanted parents to be teachers. Twice in the passage a child is in view, verses 8 and 14. The instruction assumes that children will ask and that parents will have an answer ready, a short, clear confession of what God has done. Moses was building not only a ritual but a culture of testimony.

Finally, he wanted Israel to be distinct from the nations. The LORD claims the firstborn but forbids their death; He takes a lamb instead. Israel's God is not a god who feeds on children but one who redeems them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage is prescriptive law for Israel, to be kept 'at the appointed time year after year,' verse 10, and bound to life in the land, verses 5 and 11. Christians are not required to keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread or to redeem firstborn children with silver. The New Testament treats these as shadows fulfilled in Christ, Colossians 2:16-17, and nowhere asks Gentile believers to adopt them.

Yet the passage carries principles that remain in force. The logic of verse 15, that those whom God has redeemed belong to Him, is repeated by Paul: 'You are not your own; you were bought at a price,' 1 Corinthians 6:19-20. The call to teach children what God has done becomes the charge to bring them up 'in the discipline and instruction of the Lord,' Ephesians 6:4. And the sign on the hand and forehead remains a picture of a life in which what we do and what we think are shaped by God's saving work. The form has passed; the claim and the calling have not.

debates.question: Should the sign on the hand and the symbol on the forehead be taken literally or figuratively?

views.label: A literal, physical practice
views.case: Later Jewish tradition developed tefillin, small leather boxes containing passages of Scripture, including this one, bound to the arm and forehead. By the first century the practice was established, and Jesus mentions 'phylacteries' without condemning the practice itself, only their enlargement for show, Matthew 23:5.

views.label: A vivid figure of speech
views.case: Verse 9 says the purpose is 'that the Law of the LORD is to be on your lips,' and the feast itself is called the sign. The same image in Proverbs 3:3 and 7:3, 'bind them around your neck' and 'write them on the tablet of your heart,' is plainly figurative. On this reading the hand stands for action and the forehead for thought.

debates.bearing: Either way the text insists that redemption should shape the whole of life, and Jesus' warning in Matthew 23:5 shows that an outward sign can be kept while its meaning is lost. The sign is fulfilled when God's law is written on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33.

debates.question: Does the command to give the firstborn to the LORD reflect an older practice of child sacrifice?

views.label: An earlier practice later softened
views.case: Some critical scholars read Exodus 22:29, 'You are to give Me the firstborn of your sons,' without its redemption clause and suggest that Israel's religion once demanded or tolerated the sacrifice of firstborn sons, which later law replaced with redemption. They point to the practice among Israel's neighbours, 2 Kings 3:27.

views.label: Consecration by redemption from the start
views.case: Every time the Torah explains the law in detail, it pairs the claim with redemption, Exodus 13:13, 13:15 and 34:20. The law condemns child sacrifice as an abomination, Leviticus 18:21 and Deuteronomy 12:31, and the LORD says it never entered His mind, Jeremiah 7:31. Genesis 22 already shows God providing a ram in place of the son, Genesis 22:13.

debates.bearing: The canonical text leaves no room for the sacrifice of sons. The claim is real, which is why redemption is required, but the life of the firstborn is always to be bought back. The point is that every son belongs to God and is spared only by a substitute.

study.originalLanguages:
The command of verse 2 is qaddesh, from the root that means 'holy,' in a stem that means to declare or make something holy. The LORD's explanation is two Hebrew words, li hu, 'it is Mine.' Numbers 3:13 uses the same root to describe what God did on Passover night: 'I consecrated to Myself all the firstborn in Israel.' Consecration here does not create a new status by human effort; it recognises and acts on a claim God has already made.

The 'firstborn from every womb' of verse 2 is literally 'whatever opens every womb,' peter kol rechem, and the phrase returns in verses 12 and 15. It fixes attention on the first birth, the child or animal that comes first from its mother. Luke's citation in Luke 2:23 reflects this wording in Greek, 'every male that opens the womb,' which the BSB renders 'every firstborn male.'

'Remember this day,' verse 3, is zakhor, the infinitive form used as a command, the same form that opens the Sabbath commandment, 'Remember the Sabbath day,' Exodus 20:8. In Hebrew thought remembering is not merely recalling; it is bringing the past into the present so that it shapes action. The same idea stands behind zikkaron, 'reminder,' in verse 9.

The phrase 'strength of hand,' chozeq yad, verses 3, 14 and 16, and 'mighty hand,' yad chazaqah, verse 9, come from chazaq, 'to be strong.' The same root is used for the hardening of Pharaoh's heart, Exodus 14:4, where the BSB footnote gives 'stiffen or strengthen.' Verse 15 adds another hardening word, hiqshah, 'stubbornly refused,' from qashah, 'to be hard.' The contest was between a hardened heart and a stronger hand.

In verse 8 the parent is to 'explain,' higgadta, from nagad, 'to tell' or 'declare.' Jewish tradition drew the name of its Passover liturgy, the Haggadah, from this verb.

The verb 'present' in verse 12 is he'evarta, literally 'cause to pass over' to the LORD. The same verb is used in Leviticus 18:21 and 2 Kings 16:3 for making children pass through the fire as a sacrifice. Israel's law uses the pagan language of dedication but fills it with a different meaning: the child passes over to the LORD and is bought back alive.

Finally, the key verb of verses 13 and 15 is padah, 'to ransom.' It differs from ga'al, 'to redeem as a kinsman,' used in Exodus 6:6 and 15:13. Padah focuses on the price paid to release someone from a claim. Moses uses it of the whole exodus in Deuteronomy 7:8, 'redeemed you from the house of slavery.' Psalm 49:7 says 'No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God,' and Psalm 130:8 promises that the LORD 'will redeem Israel from all iniquity.' The Septuagint regularly renders padah with lytroo, the verb family behind lytron, the 'ransom' of Mark 10:45. The alternative in verse 13 is 'break its neck,' arafta, the same verb used for the heifer of Deuteronomy 21:4, a stark reminder that the claim will be settled one way or another.

typology.type: The firstborn claimed and redeemed, Exodus 13:13-15
typology.fulfillment: Every firstborn son in Israel belonged to the LORD and lived only because a price was paid in his place. Jesus says the Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45, and Paul that God sent His Son 'to redeem those under the law,' Galatians 4:4-5. The correspondence is real, but the direction reverses. In Israel the firstborn was bought back by a lamb or five shekels. In Christ the firstborn Son is Himself the price, and through Him believers become 'the congregation of the firstborn,' Hebrews 12:23. The type falls short because silver could redeem a son for a lifetime, but only Christ's blood ransoms for eternity, 1 Peter 1:18-19.

typology.type: The Levites taken in place of the firstborn, Numbers 3:12-13
typology.fulfillment: The law of Exodus 13 was later fulfilled in a substitution. The Levites were taken for the LORD's service in place of all Israel's firstborn, Numbers 3:41, so that one tribe stood before God for the whole people. Christ is the greater substitute who stands before God for His people as their priest, Hebrews 7:24-25, and He makes them 'a royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9. The escalation is that the Levites served in the place of Israel's firstborn, while Christ both stands in His people's place and brings them near to serve with Him. The type falls short because the Levites died and were replaced; Christ 'lives forever.'

typology.type: The donkey redeemed with a lamb, Exodus 13:13
typology.fulfillment: The unclean animal could not come to God on its own terms. It lived only if a lamb died, and otherwise it had to be destroyed. The detail is not interpreted in the New Testament, so it is best read as an illustration rather than a declared type, but it pictures the condition Paul describes: people who cannot approach God as they are and must be redeemed by the blood of a lamb without blemish, 1 Peter 1:19. It also illustrates the seriousness of the claim. There is no third option of keeping the animal unredeemed, and the choice is between a substitute and loss.

typology.type: The firstborn presented at the temple, Luke 2:22-24
typology.fulfillment: Luke tells us that Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to Jerusalem 'to present Him to the Lord,' citing the law of Exodus 13:2. The true firstborn of Israel is consecrated by the very law that commemorated the Passover. Luke mentions the offering of the poor for purification, Leviticus 12:8, but says nothing about a redemption price, keeping the focus on a son wholly given to God, much as Samuel was 'dedicated to the LORD' as long as he lived, 1 Samuel 1:28. This firstborn would not be bought back from the claim; He would fulfil it with His life.

typology.type: The sign on the hand and the forehead, Exodus 13:9 and 13:16
typology.fulfillment: The exodus was to mark Israel's hands and foreheads, its actions and thoughts. The high priest wore 'HOLY TO THE LORD' on his forehead, Exodus 28:36-38. Revelation pictures the servants of God sealed on their foreheads, Revelation 7:3, and the redeemed with the Lamb's name and His Father's name 'written on their foreheads,' Revelation 14:1, in contrast to those who receive the beast's mark on hand or forehead, Revelation 13:16. The escalation is that God's own name, not a record of His act, marks His people, and the new covenant writes His law 'on their hearts,' Jeremiah 31:33.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first through the scene Luke records in the temple. Mary and Joseph bring the child 'to present Him to the Lord,' and Luke quotes 'Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord,' Luke 2:22-23, which is Exodus 13:2. It is striking that Luke mentions the purification offering but not a redemption payment. Whatever the family actually paid, Luke's interest is in a firstborn wholly given to God. Twelve years later Jesus speaks of being in 'My Father's house,' Luke 2:49. The firstborn of Mary is the Son who belongs entirely to the Father.

It leads to Christ through the logic of ransom. The firstborn of Israel were claimed by God and bought back with a price. Jesus describes His mission in exactly those terms: 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. Paul writes that Christ Jesus 'gave Himself as a ransom for all,' 1 Timothy 2:6, and Peter that believers were redeemed 'with the precious blood of Christ,' 1 Peter 1:19. Psalm 49:7-8 had said that no human being could pay the ransom for another's life. The New Testament answers that only the one who is both man and God could.

It leads to Christ through the title firstborn itself. In Exodus the firstborn are those spared and claimed. In the New Testament the title passes to Christ in a new key. He is 'the firstborn over all creation,' Colossians 1:15, not the first created but the heir with supreme rank, as Psalm 89:27 used the word for David's royal son. He is 'the firstborn from among the dead,' Colossians 1:18, the first to rise to life that cannot die. He is 'the firstborn among many brothers,' Romans 8:29, so that those joined to Him share His status. Hebrews calls the church 'the congregation of the firstborn,' Hebrews 12:23. The firstborn claimed by God in Exodus become, in Christ, a whole people who belong to Him.

And here the pattern reverses sharply. In Egypt the firstborn of Israel lived because a lamb died. In Israel every firstborn son was bought back. But God's own firstborn was not bought back. Genesis 22 had shown Abraham, stopped at the last moment, sacrificing a ram 'in place of his son,' Genesis 22:13. God the Father did not stop. Paul says He 'did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all,' Romans 8:32. The firstborn Son became the substitute so that many sons could be brought 'to glory,' Hebrews 2:10.

It is worth guarding the reading. Not every detail of Exodus 13, such as the donkey or the frontlets, is a coded prophecy of Christ, and the New Testament does not treat them that way. The link lies in what the passage is about: a God who claims His people because He has saved them, and who redeems what He claims. That is what He has done in His Son.
study.god:
The first thing the passage shows about God is His ownership. 'It is Mine,' verse 2. The LORD does not ask for the firstborn; He states that they are already His. His claim rests on creation, for 'the whole earth is Mine,' Exodus 19:5, and on redemption, for He spared Israel's firstborn when Egypt's died, verse 15. God's rights over His people are not arbitrary. They arise from what He has made and what He has done.

It shows His holiness. To consecrate is to set apart as holy, and the firstborn were to be treated as belonging to the realm of the sacred. Yet the holiness of Israel's God is not the holiness of the gods of Canaan. He claims children and forbids their death. He demands the first and then gives it back, provided a price is paid. His holiness is unapproachable, and it is also merciful, for He provides the way back.

It shows His justice and mercy held together. The alternatives of verse 13 are stark: redeem or destroy. God's claim is not symbolic, and it must be met. But He appoints the means of meeting it, a lamb or a price, so that no firstborn son of Israel needs to die. The same God who struck down Egypt's firstborn spares Israel's, not because they deserve it but because He has made provision.

It shows His strength. The 'mighty hand' of verses 3, 9, 14 and 16 is the recurring picture of the passage. God is the one who did what Israel could not do. Pharaoh 'stubbornly refused,' verse 15, but the hand of the LORD was stronger than Pharaoh's hard heart. Isaiah would later put it this way: 'I give Egypt for your ransom, Cush and Seba in your place,' Isaiah 43:3. God is willing to overturn nations for the sake of His people.

It shows His care for generations. God does not want the exodus to die with those who saw it. He gives families a way of speaking, a question and an answer, and He expects children to be taught. He is the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the God of their children's children. His faithfulness extends to 'the coming generation... even children yet to be born,' Psalm 78:6.

For worship, the passage calls for surrender and gratitude together. Surrender, because we belong to Him and are not our own. Gratitude, because the claim comes with redemption. The right response to 'It is Mine' is not resentment but the offering Paul describes: bodies presented 'as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God,' Romans 12:1, by people who know the price at which they were bought.

crossReferences.note: The LORD takes the Levites in place of every firstborn of Israel and explains why: 'On the day I struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, I consecrated to Myself all the firstborn in Israel.' It confirms that the claim of Exodus 13:2 grows directly out of the Passover and shows how the claim was carried out.

The law fixes the practice of redemption. Every firstborn son and every firstborn unclean animal must be redeemed, and the price for a son of a month old is five shekels of silver. Exodus 13:13 had said 'you must redeem'; Numbers states the cost.

After the golden calf the covenant is renewed and the law of the firstborn is repeated almost word for word, including the donkey redeemed with a lamb and the redemption of sons. The repetition shows that the claim of Exodus 13 stands at the heart of the covenant, not on its edges.

Moses applies the language of Exodus 13:9 and 13:16 to the whole law. The words are to be on the heart, taught to children at home and on the road, tied on the hands and bound on the foreheads, and written on doorposts and gates. The sign of the exodus becomes the sign of a life shaped by all God's commands.

A child asks the meaning of the commands, and the father answers, 'We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand.' The question and answer of Exodus 13:14 grow into a full catechism, joining the exodus to the whole law.

Jesus' parents bring Him to the temple to present Him to the Lord, 'as it is written in the Law of the Lord: Every firstborn male shall be consecrated to the Lord.' Luke cites Exodus 13:2 directly. The child who fulfils the law of the firstborn is the firstborn Son of God.

Jesus says the Son of Man came 'to give His life as a ransom for many.' The redemption of the firstborn in Exodus 13:13-15 required a price to release a life claimed by God. Jesus presents His death as that price, paid not for one family's son but for many.

The psalmist states that 'No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God,' for the redemption of a life is costly and no payment can suffice. The five shekels of the firstborn law were a sign; the psalm shows that the true ransom of a life is beyond human means.

Paul calls Christ 'the firstborn over all creation' and 'the firstborn from among the dead.' The language of Exodus 13, the first to open the womb, claimed by God, passes to Christ as the heir of all things and the first to rise, so that in everything He has the preeminence.

Believers have come to Mount Zion and 'the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven.' The status once held by Israel's firstborn sons, claimed by God and spared, now belongs to the whole church through Jesus the mediator and His sprinkled blood.

The prophet asks whether the LORD would be pleased if a man offered his firstborn for his transgression, and answers that the LORD requires His people 'to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God.' It rejects the pagan misuse of the firstborn claim that Exodus 13:13 had already excluded by requiring redemption.

The redeemed stand with the Lamb on Mount Zion with His name and His Father's name 'written on their foreheads,' and they are called 'firstfruits to God and to the Lamb.' The forehead sign of Exodus 13:16 and the language of the first belonging to God meet in the redeemed people of the new creation.

study.oneStory:
From the beginning of Genesis the firstborn carried weight. Abel brought 'the firstborn of his flock,' Genesis 4:4. Yet God repeatedly set aside the natural order of birth: Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Joseph and then Ephraim over their elder brothers, Genesis 48:14. The story of Genesis kept asking who the true firstborn would be. Exodus 4:22 gave a new answer: Israel, the whole people, is God's firstborn son. Exodus 13 turns that into law for every family.

The passage looks back to the Passover and draws out its consequence. The firstborn of Israel lived because a lamb died. From now on every firstborn son would be a living reminder of that night, and every firstborn animal an offering of thanks. The exodus was not to be a single rescue that faded into memory. It was to claim the whole life of the nation, year by year and birth by birth.

It also looks forward. At Sinai the firstborn's place will be taken by the Levites, Numbers 3:12, and Israel as a whole will be called 'a kingdom of priests and a holy nation,' Exodus 19:6. The pattern of claim, redemption and service runs through the law. The prophets, facing Israel's failure, look for a greater redemption, and Isaiah hears God say, 'I give Egypt for your ransom,' Isaiah 43:3, a promise that God will pay whatever it takes to recover His people.

The story reaches its centre in Jesus. He is presented at the temple as the firstborn of Mary, Luke 2:22-23. He gives His life as a ransom, Mark 10:45. He rises as 'the firstborn from among the dead,' Colossians 1:18. Through Him, people from every nation are adopted as sons, Galatians 4:5, and become 'the congregation of the firstborn,' Hebrews 12:23.

And the story ends with a people fully marked as God's own. The sign on the hand and forehead gives way to the name of God on the foreheads of His servants, Revelation 22:4, in a city where 'they will see His face.' What Exodus 13 taught in ritual, the new creation will make plain: the redeemed belong to God entirely and forever, bought back from death by the Lamb and set apart to live in His presence.

quiz.q: Why does the LORD claim every firstborn as belonging to Him, according to this chapter?

options.text: Because He spared Israel's firstborn in Egypt when He struck down Egypt's firstborn.
options.note: Verses 14 and 15 give exactly this reason, tying the claim directly to the Passover deliverance.

options.text: Because firstborn children were considered unlucky in the ancient world.
options.note: The text gives a clear redemptive reason, not a superstition about luck.

options.text: Because Israel had more children than they could support.
options.note: The reason given is theological, tied to the exodus, not a matter of family size.

options.text: No reason is given in the text.
options.note: Verses 14 to 15 explicitly explain the reason, rooted in the Passover.

quiz.q: What must be done with a firstborn donkey, according to verse 13?

options.text: It must be redeemed with a lamb, or else its neck must be broken.
options.note: The text gives this precise alternative, redemption or a broken neck.

options.text: It must be sacrificed on the altar like any other firstborn animal.
options.note: The donkey specifically cannot simply be sacrificed; it must be redeemed or killed by breaking its neck, unlike a clean sacrificial animal.

options.text: It must be sold to a foreigner.
options.note: Selling is not the instruction given; redemption with a lamb is the stated path.

options.text: Nothing needs to be done with it.
options.note: The text is explicit that it must be redeemed or its neck broken.

quiz.q: What was to happen with every firstborn son, according to verses 13 to 15?

options.text: He must always be redeemed, never sacrificed.
options.note: Unlike animals which could be substituted with a lamb or killed, human firstborn sons were always to be redeemed.

options.text: He was to be sacrificed as an offering to the LORD.
options.note: The text explicitly rules this out; the son is redeemed, not sacrificed, distinguishing Israel from surrounding child-sacrifice practices.

options.text: He was to be given away to a Levite family.
options.note: That is not what this text instructs; redemption, likely through payment or substitution, is in view here.

options.text: Nothing was required for firstborn sons.
options.note: The text explicitly requires redemption of every firstborn son.

quiz.q: What purpose does the sign on the hand and the reminder on the forehead serve?

options.text: To keep the Law of the LORD on the people's lips and the memory of the exodus ever before them.
options.note: Verse 9 states this purpose explicitly.

options.text: To identify Israelites to Egyptian border guards.
options.note: The text gives a devotional and teaching purpose, not a practical identification function.

options.text: To ward off future plagues.
options.note: No such protective function is described; the purpose is remembrance and teaching.

options.text: The text gives no explanation for the sign.
options.note: Verse 9 gives a clear explanation.

quiz.q: How does the New Testament connect to this chapter's law of the firstborn?

options.text: Jesus is presented in the temple as an infant to fulfill this very law.
options.note: Luke 2:22-23 draws a direct line to this passage.

options.text: The New Testament never mentions the firstborn at all.
options.note: Luke's Gospel explicitly cites this law in the presentation of Jesus.

options.text: Paul rejects this law as having no ongoing significance.
options.note: Paul does not reject its significance; he draws on firstborn language to describe Christ, Colossians 1:15, 18.

options.text: It is connected only to Old Testament priestly practice with no bearing on Christ.
options.note: Luke and Colossians both draw meaningful theological lines from this law to Christ.

questions: God claimed Israel's firstborn because He had already spared them. What has God already saved in your life that you have not yet formally set apart for Him?

Israel was told to explain their redemption to their children, again and again, year after year. How intentional are you about telling the story of what God has done for you to the people who come after you?

Every firstborn son was redeemed, never sacrificed, because a substitute stood in his place. How does it change your sense of security to know Christ, the true firstborn, became the substitute so you never have to be one?
The sign was meant to be on the hand and before the eyes, impossible to forget in the course of an ordinary day. What daily habit or reminder keeps God's redemption visibly before you?

This whole chapter turns a past rescue into a present and future obligation of worship. Where is God calling you to move from simply remembering what He did to actively living differently because of it?

translationNotes.note: A sign on your hand and a reminder on your forehead is figurative language in its immediate context, closely paralleled in Deuteronomy 6:8, though later Jewish practice developed it into the literal wearing of tefillin.

Break its neck describes the alternative to redemption for an unclean animal like a donkey, which could not be offered as a sacrifice; this preserved the owner's obligation to acknowledge the LORD's claim on the firstborn even without a formal offering.
Symbol on your forehead uses different Hebrew wording than verse 9's reminder, though both describe the same enduring, visible memorial of the exodus.
